note: How to have your say with District of Squamish council. Checked against District pages on October 19, 2026. The new council is sworn in November 3, 2026.

write_to_council.who_gets_it: One email to council@squamish.ca reaches the Mayor, all six councillors and the Chief Administrative Officer.
write_to_council.mail: Mayor and Council, District of Squamish, PO Box 310, Squamish, BC V8B 0A3
write_to_council.what_happens: Unless it is about day to day operations (like a service request or a bylaw complaint), a letter sent to council@squamish.ca or to four or more council members goes on an upcoming council agenda. Operational letters go to staff for a reply, and council gets a copy.
write_to_council.about_a_scheduled_item: If your letter is about something already headed to council (a development application, a public hearing, or a report staff are still writing), it is held and attached to that item when it comes up on an agenda.
write_to_council.deadline: The District does not publish a fixed cut-off for letters. Agendas are finalized and posted typically on the Thursday before a Tuesday meeting, so a letter sent after that is unlikely to make that meeting's package. For public hearings, late letters are still gathered and circulated to council right up until the hearing closes.
write_to_council.public_record: Letters that go on an agenda become public. Your name and the town you live in are published unless you ask otherwise; other personal details are removed. Anonymous letters are not circulated, so include your name and contact information.
write_to_council.monthly_posting: Letters to council that do not go on an agenda are posted online at the end of each month.

speak_at_a_meeting.summary: There are two short chances for anyone to speak at a Regular Business Meeting without booking ahead: Unscheduled Public Attendance near the start, and Open Question Period near the end. You do not register in advance. The Chair asks who wants to speak when that part of the meeting comes up.

unscheduled_public_attendance.when: Near the start of Regular Business Meetings (item 4 on the agenda, after booked speakers).
unscheduled_public_attendance.what_topics: Only something urgent that came up after the agenda closed and cannot wait until the next regular meeting, or something tied to an item on that night's agenda that must be dealt with before the next regular meeting.
unscheduled_public_attendance.how_it_works: The Chair calls for speakers. You get up to two minutes to say what your topic is and why it is urgent. Council then votes on whether to hear you. If they agree, you get up to five minutes.
unscheduled_public_attendance.limits: No more than 15 minutes or three speakers in total, unless council agrees to more.

open_question_period.when: Near the end of Regular Business Meetings.
open_question_period.what_topics: A question about an item on that meeting's agenda or a topic discussed at the meeting.
open_question_period.how_it_works: The Chair calls for speakers. You get up to two minutes to ask your question, and council gets a chance to answer.

speak_at_a_meeting.topics_that_can_be_refused: Council can turn down a request to speak if the topic is outside the District's powers, is before the courts, is a claim for damages against the District, is about bylaw enforcement against someone, promotes a business, is about staffing or labour relations, is about a District contract or tender, or is about a freedom of information request. Speaking is also refused on a rezoning that is mostly for housing and fits the Official Community Plan, because provincial law does not allow a public hearing on those. You can still write to council.
speak_at_a_meeting.ways_to_join: In person in Council Chambers at Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue (room holds 29 people including council and staff), online through Webex (use Raise Hand), or by phone at 1-604-449-3026 (press *3 to raise your hand). The YouTube live stream is for watching only.
speak_at_a_meeting.conduct: No clapping, booing or shouting. Speak respectfully. The Chair can warn and then remove people who disrupt the meeting.

delegations.summary: You can book a slot to speak to council for up to 5 minutes (the formal name is a delegation). Send a written request to the Corporate Officer two weeks before the meeting you want. Include the names of everyone who will speak, your topic, and whether you will attend in person or online. The Mayor decides whether to approve it.
delegations.lead_time: Two weeks before the requested meeting.
delegations.time_limit: Up to five minutes at a Regular Business Meeting, unless council votes to give more. The Mayor can allow more time at Special meetings and Committee of the Whole.
delegations.how_to_apply: Use the District's Application to Appear form and attach any supporting documents. Audio visual equipment is not allowed, so send handouts with your application.
delegations.form_note: The older Application to Appear form gives a different deadline (noon on the Tuesday the week before the meeting). The current Procedure Bylaw says two weeks, so apply at least two weeks ahead to be safe.
delegations.proclamations: Groups asking for a proclamation must send a local representative to the meeting, and get up to five minutes. Contact Legislative Services at 604-815-5005.

public_hearings.summary: A public hearing is your formal chance to tell council what you think of a rezoning or Official Community Plan change before they vote on it. Hearings usually start at 6 p.m. and are now held as part of a council meeting.
public_hearings.written_submissions: Email hearing@squamish.ca, or drop it at the front counter of Municipal Hall by 3 p.m. on the day of the hearing, or hand it in at the hearing. Submissions are published in the agenda package.
public_hearings.speaking: Speak in person, by Webex or by phone. Each speaker gets three minutes per turn, which the Chair can adjust. Start with your name and your address or neighbourhood, and say whether you speak for yourself, a business or a group. Talk to council about the bylaw itself; there is no debating other speakers. The Chair calls three times for more speakers before closing.
public_hearings.big_hearings: Large hearings are sometimes moved to Brennan Park Recreation Centre. Phone and Webex are not available for hearings held there, so plan to attend or write in.
public_hearings.after_it_closes: Once the hearing closes, council cannot receive anything more from the public on that bylaw. Letters sent afterward are filed but not given to council.
public_hearings.variance_permits: For development variance permits and development permits with variances, the process is similar: the Chair invites the public to speak, and emailed submissions to hearing@squamish.ca must arrive by 3 p.m. on the day of the meeting.

watch.summary: Council meetings stream live on YouTube and stay online afterward. Regular Business Meetings are in Council Chambers at Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue, starting at 6 p.m., usually on the first and third Tuesday of the month.
watch.agenda_timing: Regular meeting agendas are usually posted the Thursday before a Tuesday meeting. Committee of the Whole and Special meeting agendas are posted when finalized.
watch.captions: Use YouTube's CC button for live captions.
watch.upcoming: Inaugural meeting November 3, 2026 at 6 p.m.; Regular meetings November 17, December 1 and December 15, 2026.

contacts.members_note: As of October 19, 2026 the District's council page still lists the outgoing council. Individual District email addresses for the new mayor and the five new councillors have not been published yet. Until they are, use council@squamish.ca, which reaches every member. Eric Andersen is the only returning member, and his District address is published. Current members' addresses follow the pattern first initial plus last name at squamish.ca, but the District has not confirmed addresses for new members, so do not assume them.

neighbourhoods_source_note: Names follow the District's Evacuation Zones map and the neighbourhood and sub-area plans in the Official Community Plan. The Squamish Valley and Paradise Valley are outside District boundaries (Squamish-Lillooet Regional District), so they are not listed.
